name: Grounded goal agent: the engine that answers and works on a person's goals from their own material, and the executor that runs their queued AI tasks
scoped_purpose: Use for answering chat turns about a person's or team's goals, carrying out requested changes, running queued and recurring AI tasks to a written standard, doing long autonomous work through a deep runner, and escalating decisions to the right person. Intentionally avoids: being a chat interface (consumers render it), owning goal data or storage (the consumer's adapters do), holding any one organization's names, rules or data, being a hosted service, and doing work a person should decide.
knowledge: Agent loop research (reason and act, plan and execute, verification against a written goal); retrieval-augmented generation and context selection; evaluation of language-model systems; Quest's model of quests, goals, notes, asks and AI tasks; the operating principle "AI acts first, humans confirm"; Joshua's evolvable structure that optimizes intent.
measures_of_success: People's goals move through delegated work; tasks and replies need no correction; operators accept the cost; Joshua can steer by reviewing metrics without needing to read code. Standing conditions: Chat turns that pass their rubric (grounded facts, right handling, exact changes) at a cost per passing turn the operator accepts; queued tasks that meet their written goal; no unrequested writes and no human-only step taken alone; no data across scope; every part measured and selected by its metric.
parameters: One configuration per lane: the consumer's adapters (retrieval, cards, conversations, escalation, deep runner), model tiers and providers, personas, budgets and schedules, and the implementation selected for each swappable solution.
inputs: A person's message or a queued task, the quest and goal it concerns, and the sources the adapters reach.
outputs: A reply, a task result reported against its goal, a decision-request for a person, or files and records changed as requested.
effects: Writes to Quest and other systems through their APIs and tools; model and search spend; context cards and conversation memory kept for later turns.
usage_notes: Two entry points share one brain: the importable core (`Orchestrator`) for chat and other hosts, and the runner (a lane that polls, claims, runs, escalates and reports) for queued work. A terminal chat drives the same brain. Every specific comes through configuration; nothing about a consumer is built in.

name: Cost-aware message router
scoped_purpose: Use for: deciding, for each incoming user message, whether to answer, call a tool, start a deep run, ask for confirmation or ask a clarifying question, and which tool with which arguments. Avoid: carrying out the chosen route, gathering evidence, or composing the reply, which other solutions own.
milestones: 1. Routing correctness over the classification cases: re-recorded for every arm after the planner confirms before sending a destructive request to deep and reads "where I am now" as a current-state update.
knowledge: Past failures were a paraphrased current-state update sent to deep or answered, and a mass destructive request sent to deep without a confirm. A cheap single call that returns only a label cannot gather evidence, brief a deep run or ground an answer, so a label alone is not a decision. A pre-route stage is owned by another solution and is measured here only as routing.
measures_of_success: The route, the tool, the filled arguments and every tool of a multi-step request match the labelled expectation on held-out cases. No confirming argument appears on a first destructive ask, and no tool call appears where none was requested.
parameters: The message text, the model tier used for the routing call (configurable per deployment), and the planner profile that selects the planner variant. The tool catalogue offered to the router is also a configuration choice.
inputs: The user message, a short view of the quest in play (title and outcome), recent conversation, and the catalogue of tools the router may name.
outputs: A routing decision: one of answer, tool, deep, confirm or clarify, plus the ordered tool calls with their arguments when the route is tool.
effects: The routing call spends model tokens. Nothing is executed: no tool runs, no deep run starts and nothing is written.
usage_notes: Call once per message before any execution. Treat confirm and clarify as stops that hand control back to a person. A cheap first stage may settle a clear request, but anything it does not settle must reach the full planner.
verdict_detail: within the stated margin of pre_route_then_planner: pass rate inside 10 percentage points and spend inside 15% (sampled, model-judged runs move that much between re-runs), so the metric does not separate them

name: Grounded chat turn handler
scoped_purpose: Use for: replying to a user's chat message with facts held in their own account, handled inline or handed to a deep run as the request needs, with exactly the changes asked for. Avoid: bulk or scheduled work with no conversational reply, and replies that state facts no read supports.
milestones: 1. Share of dev chat cases passed by the cheapest tier (haiku): 100%, at a cost per passing turn of a few cents. Set by Joshua on 2026-10-19; no dollar ceiling per turn is set.
knowledge: Recorded misses repeat: asking which quest or for data the quest already holds, proposing instead of writing when the request was unambiguous, stating an unsupported fact, and ending a multi-step request with a queued task and no report of what is unfinished. A turn can take many model calls, so cost per passing turn matters. A rubric judged by a model is not yet calibrated against human verdicts, and a small sample cannot rank two implementations.
measures_of_success: On a rich, realistic disposable account, hard deterministic checks pass first (reply text, routing, side effects, tools called) and a judge finds every rubric item met. Repeated runs of the same case agree. Standing conditions: Minimise side effects that were not requested, unsupported claims, needless questions about data the account already holds, and model calls per passing turn.
parameters: The model tier or pinned model for the chat, the model-call budget for an evaluation run, and the quest the turn is scoped to.
inputs: The user message, the conversation so far, the account's quests and data reachable through read tools, and the context the host supplies.
outputs: The reply text, the routing taken (inline or delegated), the tools called, and any queued or delegated work with its status.
effects: Reads account data, may write quest data the user asked for, may queue a deep run, and spends model tokens.
usage_notes: Use the evaluation arm only against a disposable world, never real data. Run the offline validity arm first to confirm the checks can tell a good reply from none, then the live arm on a small stratified sample.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Quest change executor
scoped_purpose: Use for: carrying out a requested change to a quest (goals, habits, outcomes, notes, experiments) with the right tool and arguments, including multi-step requests. Avoid: writing on an ambiguous or merely informational message, deleting without confirmation, and requests that need a computer rather than a quest tool.
knowledge: A cheap pre-route that settles clear requests for a direct tool and the planner alone reach the same outcomes, with the pre-route spending somewhat fewer tokens, so the choice is a tie kept by a stated reason. A direct tool path alone is cheaper but cannot do multi-step or ambiguous requests. Sharing a fact is not a request to record it.
measures_of_success: The in-memory quest state after the run equals the expected state: the right tool with the right arguments, every step done, nothing written on an ambiguous or sharing message, and an unconfirmed delete leaving the record in place.
parameters: The pre-route selection (pre-route or planner alone), the set of tools allowed to run directly, the model tier for the routing and planning calls, and the host's override of the selection.
inputs: The user message, the quest's current record (state, goals, habits, outcomes, experiments), and the tool registry with its schemas.
outputs: The resulting quest state and a reply that reports what was done.
effects: Mutates the quest through registry tools and spends model tokens. A deep run is not started by this solution.
usage_notes: Direct tools should be only plain, reversible creates and finds whose every argument the message supplies. Anything destructive, outward or ambiguous must go to the planner. A host with no pre-router runs the planner alone.
verdict_detail: within the stated margin of qar_orchestrator: pass rate inside 10 percentage points and spend inside 15% (sampled, model-judged runs move that much between re-runs), so the metric does not separate them

name: Multi-source evidence retriever
scoped_purpose: Use for: reading targeted sources (files, databases, workspace documents and chat, MCP servers, the Quest API) so the planner can ground a decision or answer. Avoid: writing to any source, searching the open web (a separate solution), and reading beyond the configured roots or allowlists.
knowledge: Per-source adapters are complementary sources, not alternatives, so a composite stack is the unit that is ranked. Some sources do not search: a drive has no search so its policy is to list and read, a notion source locates by row, and an MCP result measures plumbing because the server does the search. Fixtures are written rather than recorded and keyword gathering misses paraphrases. A remote search must be scoped because a composite broadcasts unscoped requests.
measures_of_success: The right document is found near the top for questions over a representative corpus, the answer is readable, and a broken source returns an error observation while the other sources still answer.
parameters: Per source: the root or base address, an alias for namespacing, token provider or credential source, allowlists of tools or databases, cache lifetime, size and time budgets. At composition level: the ordered list of member adapters.
inputs: A read request (path with optional line range or heading), a regular-expression search with an optional scope, or a structured query specification; plus discovery calls to list and describe sources and operations.
outputs: Observation values carrying text, a path or source label, and a kind, with error observations in place of exceptions.
effects: Read-only network and file access, in-memory caching, and wall-clock spent on requests. No writes to any source.
usage_notes: Wire members into the composite and let the planner use discovery before reading. Always scope remote searches and keep credentials injected, never embedded. Treat every adapter as never raising.
verdict_detail: passes more cases than first_three

name: Bounded web research
scoped_purpose: Use for: answering questions that need current public web information, with snippet-first search, focused page reading, caching and a spending limit. Avoid: crawling arbitrary private addresses, dumping whole pages into context, and using paid search on every ordinary corpus read.
milestones: 1. Right-passage rate and search spend: web_search_live recorded for each vendor as its key is configured, with spend per right answer compared across vendors, then live cases grown to the next rung of the ladder.
knowledge: Dedicated search APIs return titles, links and snippets quickly and cheaply; provider-native grounding needs no extra key but costs more at volume. Web access is kept out of the composite retriever because broadcasting would fire paid searches on every corpus grep. Live measurement covers only the vendors configured in the environment, and fixture payloads prove handling, not relevance or freshness.
measures_of_success: An answer phrase appears in the observation the planner would see for public factual questions, at low spend per correct answer, with backend failures falling back cleanly.
parameters: Backend selection and fallback order, vendor keys and base addresses, number of results, per-page token budget, cache lifetime, and the page-fetch fallback provider.
inputs: One or more search queries, or a page address with a focus phrase.
outputs: One compact observation of title, link and snippet per hit with citable links, or focused page passages capped to a budget; an error observation on failure.
effects: Outbound network requests, spend on paid search calls, and cache writes in memory. Fetches are restricted to safe addresses.
usage_notes: Search first and fetch a page only when a snippet is not enough. Configure at least one backend and a fallback, and keep web access as its own planner read key rather than inside the composite.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Tiered model provider layer
scoped_purpose: Use for: running planning and answering calls on the right vendor and tier, retrying transient errors and stepping down a tier on quota exhaustion. Avoid: choosing which task needs which tier (callers decide) and prompt content itself.
knowledge: Models route by name prefix to their vendor; a vendor with no key is simply not registered. Transient errors deserve bounded retries while quota errors deserve a lower tier, and a give-up records a process-wide outage. Price tables count input tokens only, and no live latency or pass rate per tier has been recorded. Keyless subscription-based execution through a local command-line tool is an option where no API key exists.
measures_of_success: The right provider serves each model name, a quota error falls to a working tier, transient errors are retried the right number of times, and cost estimates order tiers correctly, all on offline cases.
parameters: Model backend selection, per-tier model pins, vendor keys and base addresses, retry count and base delay, and the registry that maps tiers to model identifiers.
inputs: A planning request (prompt plus a forced tool schema) or an answering request (messages plus an optional system prompt), with a model name or tier and optional step and reasoning hints.
outputs: A raw decision dictionary for planning, answer text for answering, and a live list of available model identifiers; errors are formatted for humans.
effects: Network calls to model vendors (or a spawned local command-line process), spend, and a process-wide outage marker after a give-up.
usage_notes: Wrap vendors in the multi-provider and let the registry resolve tiers. Prefer the cheapest tier that passes the task's own evaluation, and pin a vendor only deliberately.
verdict_detail: passes more cases than single_provider

name: Bounded autonomous work runner
scoped_purpose: Use for: doing open-ended or heavy work to a written, checkable done-standard under a turn and cost bound, on the cheapest runner that can make the edit. Avoid: tiny or conversational requests that need no autonomy, and work with no checkable done-standard.
knowledge: The full agent is the right tool for open-ended work and wasteful for a small edit, so cheap rungs are tried first and verified, with escalation on failure. The two full runners tie on the contract. Cost per success is not yet measured because the scenarios script the process edge. A wrong stop loses work, which is why stall review is a separate solution.
measures_of_success: Each scripted outcome (met, silent no-op, paused on a human with a decision id, partial or crashed, missing binary) is reported in the common shape and no scenario raises. The goal contract's met-versus-limit, stop and resume rules hold.
parameters: Goal text with its done-standard, brief, model, maximum turns, working directory, binary or agent command, timeout, a per-call context preamble and the ordered runner ladder.
inputs: A goal, a brief with gathered context, and optional progress emitter and run identifier for tagging retries.
outputs: A result stating whether the goal was met, the output text, and error or pause details such as a decision id.
effects: Spawns worker processes, edits files or calls operations on the runner's behalf, spends tokens, and emits execution progress events.
usage_notes: Order the ladder from cheapest to most capable and let the verifier decide whether to escalate. Pass a stable run identifier across retries. A runner must never raise.
verdict_detail: passes as many cases as acp_runner at spend within 10% (or lower), so the metric does not separate them

name: Run liveness reviewer
scoped_purpose: Use for: deciding from a worker's live activity log whether a run should still be running, so stuck runs stop and slow-but-alive ones continue. Avoid: stopping on elapsed time alone, and using it to judge whether the goal was achieved.
milestones: 1. Stop-or-continue verdict accuracy with false stops counted apart: zero false stops for live_reviewer at each re-score, as a small dev run.
knowledge: A wrong stop loses work that was about to land, so the reviewer fails open: any problem reaching or reading it means keep running. A quiet parent log while a subagent works is real work. Builds, tests and downloads look idle but are alive. A rule floor written with the cases in view is an optimistic ceiling for a rule, not a blind result.
measures_of_success: Verdicts match hand-labelled logs, with no false stops and few missed stops, and the unreadable-verdict case degrades to keep running.
parameters: Review interval, review model, call timeout, and the prompt template with elapsed time, idle time and log tail.
inputs: Elapsed run time, time since the log last changed, and a tail of the session activity.
outputs: A verdict of stop or keep running with a one-sentence reason, and a usage-limit signal when relevant.
effects: One small model call per review for a model-based reviewer; the verdict triggers a stop of the worker.
usage_notes: Review periodically, skip the model when a subagent is plainly working, and treat an unreadable verdict as keep running. Re-score with held-out logs whenever the prompt changes.
verdict_detail: within the stated margin of rule_floor: pass rate inside 10 percentage points and spend inside 15% (sampled, model-judged runs move that much between re-runs), so the metric does not separate them

name: Bounded reversible file writer
scoped_purpose: Use for: letting an automated agent change files inside one configured root with every change recoverable. Avoid: writes outside the root, to secret-like or binary files, and any unbacked destructive overwrite.
knowledge: Containment must resolve symlinks and parent references before testing the boundary, and the read side and write side should share one implementation. Backups belong outside the corpus rather than relying on version control. The binary-extension and secret-name lists are fixed in code, and concurrent writers are not covered.
measures_of_success: All boundary cases (traversal, absolute and sibling-prefix paths, symlink escape, protected names, size and create limits) are refused with the outside untouched, ordinary writes succeed, and an overwrite leaves a readable backup. Standing conditions: Guarantee no write lands outside the configured root and every overwrite keeps a recoverable copy. Refuse oversize, protected and out-of-policy writes without side effects.
parameters: Root directory, backup directory, whether backups are enabled, whether creating new files is allowed, and the maximum bytes per write.
inputs: A path relative to the root and the full replacement content; a read request for the current content.
outputs: A write result stating success, whether the file was created, bytes written, where the backup went and any error; the current text on read.
effects: Creates or replaces a file under the root and writes a backup copy outside it. Nothing changes when the result is not ok.
usage_notes: Constructing the writer is the act of granting write access, so wire it only deliberately. Handle a refused result as an ordinary outcome and escalate rather than retry around it.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Allowlisted operation writer
scoped_purpose: Use for: running one named mutating operation on an external tool server, only if it is explicitly allowed. Avoid: read-side use, operations not on the write allowlist, and repeating an operation.
knowledge: A write allowlist is separate from any read allowlist, so being readable grants nothing here. A refused operation must never touch the server. Names are alias-prefixed so servers do not collide, and the planner may pass the prefixed or bare form. Real servers are not exercised in the offline arm.
measures_of_success: An allowed call reaches the client once with exact arguments, a disallowed call makes zero server calls, and server errors and dead connections come back as failed results with details recorded. Standing conditions: Guarantee that exactly the requested mutation runs once, and that anything off the allowlist is refused with no server call. Make every attempt auditable.
parameters: Server alias and connection spec, the write allowlist of tool names, and the timeout.
inputs: An operation name (prefixed or bare) and its arguments; a discovery call for the writable catalogue.
outputs: A write result with success, error and an audit detail of the tool, arguments and whether it executed; a list of writable operations with schemas.
effects: One mutating call on the external server when allowed; no effect when refused.
usage_notes: List writable operations first, pick at most one, and escalate when refused or failed. Keep the write allowlist narrower than the read one.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Human decision escalation channel
scoped_purpose: Use for: surfacing a step only a person may take, with enough detail to decide, and stopping until they respond. Avoid: deciding whether a step needs a human (the router does that) and unaddressed or duplicate asks.
knowledge: An ask filed with no assignee once sat in nobody's queue, which is worse than failing visibly, so the sink raises instead. Assignee falls back from explicit to configured default to the quest owner. A deadline default and a review link make asks actionable. Delivery is a contract, not a quality that improves.
measures_of_success: Every escalation produces an addressed decision with kind, hold-or-proceed default, deadline and review link as given, duplicates are handled, and backend failures are visible.
parameters: The default assignee, default deadline in hours, and the escalation's summary, kind, quest, assignee, default on silence, deadline and review link.
inputs: An escalation value describing the human-only step.
outputs: A decision identifier the caller reports back.
effects: Creates a decision request in the host's task system; the run holds by default until answered.
usage_notes: Escalate once per decision, include a review link when a draft or preview exists, and keep the default on silence at hold unless the host says otherwise.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Mode-aware progress surfacing
scoped_purpose: Use for: deciding which run events a user sees, by mode: everything while watching live, only milestones in the background. Avoid: deciding which events the orchestrator emits, and any logic that can break the run.
knowledge: Messaging policy lives in one place, the sinks, so the orchestrator only emits. Chatter such as planning and reading is dropped in the background so users are not spammed. A detach hands a live run to the background sink. This scores the sinks, not what the orchestrator emits.
measures_of_success: Each mode surfaces exactly its stated set, order is preserved, a mid-run detach switches policy cleanly, and a failing stream or callback is swallowed. Standing conditions: Ensure live mode shows every event in order and background mode shows only result, decision, milestone, context, tokens and done. Never let a broken stream or callback stop the run.
parameters: The mode, the forward function for the live stream, and the per-event callbacks for the background sink.
inputs: A progress event with a type and text, and the current mode.
outputs: None returned; surfaced events reach the consumer's stream or callbacks.
effects: Calls consumer callbacks or pushes to a stream; swallows their failures.
usage_notes: Pick the sink by mode, fan out when a live run may detach, and keep sinks free of side effects beyond forwarding.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Cross-conversation recall store
scoped_purpose: Use for: resolving a short or anaphoric message against the current conversation, and recalling relevant earlier conversations of the same user or team as prompt context. Avoid: searching documents or cards (that is context selection), and returning any other user's conversation under any circumstance.
knowledge: Recall must be relevance-first over the whole history, with recency only a small boost and a small floor of the newest conversations, because time cutoffs lost old but relevant threads. Scanning every file in full does not scale, so a cheap per-file digest shortlists candidates and only a capped few are fully loaded. Paraphrased questions that share no words with a past thread remain a known gap for term-based ranking.
measures_of_success: The conversation a person means is returned among the first few results, including old ones and paraphrases, no conversation from another user or outside the requested scope ever appears, and call cost stays flat as history grows.
parameters: Per call: the query text, a scope (user, team, since, participant), an optional conversation id to exclude, the maximum number of conversations, a character budget, and optional opaque filters such as a time range. Construction takes a corpus root and a sessions directory.
inputs: A natural-language query or the latest user message, a scope dictionary, and for the current-conversation call a conversation id and the number of recent turns considered.
outputs: A conversation context holding rendered text slices from the selected conversations, plus a degraded note when a hard filter matched nothing and the store fell back to relevance only.
effects: None beyond outputs apart from in-memory caches of per-file digests and parsed conversations; it never writes conversations and never raises, returning an empty context on failure.
usage_notes: Call before planning so that follow-up messages become self-contained goals. Always pass the scope of the asking user so isolation is enforced; add a backend by implementing the same protocol rather than changing callers.
verdict_detail: passes more cases than most_recent

name: Context card selector
scoped_purpose: Use for: choosing which stored context cards (files, collections, conversations, learned topics) are rendered into a prompt before the model plans. Avoid: storing cards (see persist-cards), judging whether the selected context is sufficient, and any selection that needs a model call on the hot path unless the deadline allows it.
milestones: 1. Context selection ranking accuracy: top-1 and top-3 recorded on the same tasks with the production embedder and with real misrouted tasks.
knowledge: Keyword scoring over file names, symbols and docstring summaries beats blind text search, and removing the docstring text hurts it, so the orientation text earns its place. Semantic search recovers paraphrases but on the measured proxy it added recall only past the top few and never improved rank, so its advantage is unproven. Card quality has its own incident history: an open confidence gate selects a card for any query, and learned cards need their collection references resolved fresh at read time.
measures_of_success: The right file is first or in the first few over symptom, paraphrase and hard task shapes, an unrelated query selects nothing, learned collection cards come back with fresh rows and without leaking other cards, and a warm hint helps an agent find the file faster than cold search.
parameters: Per assembler: confidence threshold, maximum cards in view, number of generated queries, vector similarity floor, whether a model review or consolidation pass is on, and a deadline carried in the call metadata. Arms are chosen by configuration (a vector store setting selects the hybrid).
inputs: The task text, optional metadata (recent item usage hint, assembly deadline, scope), and the configured card repository, vector store, optional model provider and reference resolvers.
outputs: An assembled context: rendered context view, card ids in relevance order, card metadata, stale file list, sources and an optional model-tier hint; empty when nothing is confident enough.
effects: Optional best-effort write-back of outcomes through record, and lazy index refresh on use; it never raises and an empty result lets the caller proceed without context.
usage_notes: Wire the hybrid when a vector store exists, otherwise the keyword store; wrap or compose arms rather than editing them. Put per-agent preferences in a wrapper, and keep selection deterministic enough that identical inputs render identically.
verdict_detail: passes as many cases as idf_docstrings at spend within 10% (or lower), so the metric does not separate them

name: Context card persistence backend
scoped_purpose: Use for: storing, listing, updating and deleting context cards durably across a local folder, a vector database or the Quest backend with the same behaviour. Avoid: deciding which cards are relevant (that is select-context) and any backend-specific logic leaking into card handling.
milestones: 1. Card repository conformance: the same case set passed against a Qdrant server and the dev Quest API.
knowledge: Persistence is a boundary: card logic lives in the store and a backend only stores and fetches. A listing that silently truncated at a page limit once made a backend fail the volume case. Backend errors must be loud and counted, not swallowed, and card identity is the pair of scope and id so the same id may exist privately and in a team.
measures_of_success: Every conformance case passes on every backend: round trip, overwrite, no loss at volume and across pages, no duplicate, delete including after restart, concurrent writers, change stamp and tolerance of bad input. Standing conditions: Lose no card, create no duplicate, and behave the same on every backend, including after restart, under concurrent writers and across paged listings.
parameters: Backend choice and connection (folder path; vector collection, embedder and vector size or server url; Quest base url, key, timeout and scope), plus the optional scope used for tenant isolation.
inputs: Card ids and card dictionaries for write (a card as defined in docs/context-assembly.md, What a context card is: id, name, keywords, summary and description, pinned files, typed content references, provenance, usage, scope tags and origin); ids for read, delete and exists.
outputs: Load-all returns a mapping of id to card, read returns a card or nothing, write and delete return success flags, and revision returns a change stamp used to invalidate caches.
effects: Durable writes to the chosen store (atomic files, vector points embedded at write time, or API calls), and for the API backend logged and counted errors.
usage_notes: Pick the backend by where the cards must live and inject it into the card store; every backend must pass the same conformance cases, so none is better when it conforms. Add a backend by implementing the protocol and a harness. A card's fields, its id rules and what is not a card are defined once in docs/context-assembly.md, What a context card is; docs/context-card-stores.md covers stores, mounts and copies.
verdict_detail: passes as many cases as filesystem, qdrant at spend within 10% (or lower), so the metric does not separate them

name: Semantic vector index
scoped_purpose: Use for: finding cards or snippets by meaning, including paraphrases, with an index that keeps itself current. Avoid: exact-identifier search (use keyword or content search) and acting as the system of record for cards.
milestones: 1. Semantic recall and query latency: query latency measured against a Qdrant server at the same corpus size.
knowledge: Embedding only the start of a long item loses facts near its end, an incident pinned by a failing case. Latency of an embedded local store is not the latency of a networked server, and the local embedder is smaller than the deployed one. Multi-tenant isolation by payload filter is preferred over a collection per tenant.
measures_of_success: The labelled card is among the first few results for most questions, mostly paraphrases, and median and tail latency stay under the interactive caps at the stated corpus size.
parameters: Collection prefix, storage path or server url, embedder and vector size, and per-call scope and number of results.
inputs: A query string and optional scope for search; item dictionaries with id, text, payload and fingerprint for upsert and sync.
outputs: Ranked hits with id, score, text and payload for search; counts for sync and count; the number deleted for eviction.
effects: Writes embedded points to the collection and re-embeds only items whose fingerprint changed; never raises, returning empty or zero on error.
usage_notes: Call sync on every run to keep the index fresh, pass a scope so private points stay private, and treat unscoped points as shared. Add a second store by implementing the protocol.
verdict_detail: passes as many cases as memory_cosine at spend within 10% (or lower), so the metric does not separate them

name: Feedback-to-guidance loop
scoped_purpose: Use for: turning human corrections into stored guidance that is shown on later relevant turns so the same correction is not needed twice. Avoid: turning a one-off request into a permanent rule, and showing guidance that does not bear on the turn.
knowledge: Remembering everything gives perfect recall but turns one-time requests into permanent rules and crowds every prompt, so a ledger separating standing from one-off corrections is needed. The current weakness is precision: with no relevance cut below the card limit, an unrelated rule is shown while room remains. Guidance enters the system prompt as behaviour to follow, not optional context.
measures_of_success: After a standing correction is stored, the next relevant turn shows it, corrections that do not bear on the turn are not shown, and one-off requests are not promoted.
parameters: Cards directory, optional dynamic guidance loader, vector store, provider and model for relevance filtering, a card manager factory, and the number of cards selected per turn.
inputs: A user message and caller scope metadata for selection; correction text, author, location and run dispositions for the ledger.
outputs: A list of guidance cards with bodies for the applicable-guidance block; a catalog and single card reads on demand.
effects: The ledger records observations and writes guidance cards on standing corrections; selection itself is read-only; never raises.
usage_notes: Wire the provider into the orchestrator so selection runs once before planning; rank by relevance when the card limit has room, add a vector or model filter where precision matters.
verdict_detail: passes more cases than dump_all; passes more cases than no_memory

name: Live messaging channel transport
scoped_purpose: Use for: receiving and sending messages on a live external chat channel through a gateway, with each message delivered once and in order. Avoid: operating the gateway itself, approving permissions on its behalf, and polling history that the live event stream already delivers.
knowledge: The gateway's wire shapes were written from documentation without a live gateway, so the evidence is conformance to tolerant guesses. The gateway has had a serious authentication-token vulnerability, so the bridge requires a patched version, disabled skills and plugins, and never approves permissions itself. Approvals belong to the host's decision flow.
measures_of_success: Offline cases pass: ordered inbound messages, spelling drift in keys, ignored non-message and malformed events, graceful wire failure and dead gateway, long-poll clamp, attachments, correct send arguments and ids, only allowed tools called, and idempotent close. Standing conditions: Deliver every message exactly once and in order, survive malformed events and gateway failure without raising, and restrict calls to the allowed tool set.
parameters: Token file, channel name, whether to fetch attachments, and the receive timeout in seconds.
inputs: For receive, a timeout; for send, an outbound reply with chat reference, text and optional reply-to id.
outputs: An inbound batch (messages with ids, chat references, text and attachments, a healthy flag and any error) and a send result with success and message id.
effects: Network calls to the gateway for long-poll, send and attachment fetch; close tears down the held connection. Every failure is returned as a value, never raised.
usage_notes: Run the gateway locked down as documented, call receive in a loop, treat an empty batch as normal, and add a channel through gateway configuration or a second transport implementing the protocol.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Learned-operation fast path
scoped_purpose: Use for: recognising a repeated, previously successful tool operation and replaying it before any context search, filling only the arguments. Avoid: replaying on a near miss or lookalike write, running a tool for plain chat, and replacing the normal path when no recipe matches.
milestones: 1. Fast-path hit rate and parity: recipe_replay and planner_only recorded live through the claude CLI, with hit rate and cost compared against the offline arm.
knowledge: A lookalike request must never trigger a write, so replay carries a guard for mutating operations and a minimum match score. The offline arm uses a rule model written with the cases in view, so it proves the engine, not a real model's judgment. Recipes are learned only from successes.
measures_of_success: Right tool and arguments on a repeat, no tool on a near miss or on chat, a large share of repeats served from recipes, and fewer model calls than the planner-only path at the same pass rate.
parameters: The recipe store path (or none for memory only), the minimum match score, scope tags for learning and matching, and the planner model tier.
inputs: A user request and the registry of available tools.
outputs: The reply text and exit reason of the run, with the tool executed and its arguments when a recipe fired.
effects: Learns a new recipe after a successful operation and rewrites the recipe file atomically under a lock; may execute a tool.
usage_notes: Enable by configuring a recipe store on the orchestrator; compare against a planner-only run on the same tasks before trusting it, and keep mutating operations behind the guard.
verdict_detail: same pass rate as planner_only_offline at 24% lower spend

name: Minimal-intervention run overseer
scoped_purpose: Use for: a cheap high-quality model watching a compact digest of a run and sending one tiny signal only when it drifts, wastes reads, has enough to answer, or needs deep execution or a human. Avoid: frequent interventions, routine work escalated to a human, and reading full operation bodies.
milestones: 1. Overseer digest evidence and signal correctness: the overseer_signals live_model arm recorded.
knowledge: The digest must show the evidence each label depends on, shedding old history operations first and prior escalations last so the refusal rule keeps its evidence. A failure must degrade to proceed, and a degraded flag lets a caller retry at another tier so a silent overseer is distinguishable from a healthy one. Human escalation is for genuine forks only, since routine work is AI-doable.
measures_of_success: Correct signal on hand-labelled contrast scenarios, mostly proceed when the run is healthy, the digest holds the deciding evidence, and a bad or missing verdict degrades to proceed. Standing conditions: Keep interventions few and each one correct, keep the digest and the overseer's own token cost small, and never change a run's outcome except through an explicit signal.
parameters: The overseer model tier, the digest character budget, the thresholds for when to consult, and the provider.
inputs: A digest string built from the user message, goal, step counters, the plan, recent conversation, prior escalations and recent operation summaries.
outputs: An overseer signal: proceed, redirect with a short hint, answer now, escalate to deep execution, or escalate to a human, with a one-sentence reason and a degraded flag.
effects: One small model call per consult; the signal may redirect, stop reading, or hand off the run. No other writes; never raises.
usage_notes: Consult at intervals rather than every step, treat a degraded proceed as a reason to retry at another tier, and keep the prompt and digest compact.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Source-change staleness detector
scoped_purpose: Use for: deciding which context cards no longer match their source files after edits or deletions. Avoid: judging whether a card's meaning is still right, and paying a full hash on every check when speed matters more.
knowledge: A modification time and size pair is cheap but misses an edit that keeps the size and restores the time, and flags a merely touched file. A content hash is exact but costs a read. The production store keeps a fast path on modification time, accepting one deliberate miss.
measures_of_success: High precision and recall over synthetic mutation cases: edits and deletes flagged, untouched and merely touched files not flagged. Standing conditions: Flag every changed or deleted file and no unchanged file, and keep the check cheap.
parameters: The repository root for fingerprints and whether a git blob id is used when available.
inputs: A pinned file path (or a set of paths) and the current tree.
outputs: Whether the file is stale, and the stale card list for the path.
effects: None beyond reading files and computing hashes; fingerprints are written when a card is written.
usage_notes: Pin a fingerprint when a card is written, ask on assemble, and decide per deployment whether mtime-preserving edits matter enough to hash every time.
verdict_detail: passes more cases than mtime_size

name: Budgeted prompt assembler
scoped_purpose: Use for: composing each prompt from its parts so it fits a budget derived from the model window and cost per call, with no duplicated blocks. Avoid: judging whether the content is the right content (selection and evidence gathering own that) and unbounded concatenation.
knowledge: An incident showed prompts growing past what the cheapest tier tolerates, so budgets are derived from the cheapest tier's window, a stated share and the cost per call. The shares and cost caps are policy to be confirmed by a human, and the fixtures are generated filler at incident sizes, not real content.
measures_of_success: Every assembly point stays under budget on all fixtures with reported headroom, and no block appears twice. Standing conditions: Keep the size at each assembly point under its budget, keep duplicated blocks at zero, and leave headroom under healthy, incident and production-sized inputs.
parameters: Per assembly point budgets from the budget inputs file, the autopilot brief token budget, and the fitting policy for goal prompts.
inputs: The planner message, transcript, context view and gathered results; the autopilot batch parts; a context-update bundle; and a goal, brief and preamble for a deep prompt.
outputs: The assembled prompt string for each assembly point.
effects: None beyond the prompt; fitting may drop or shorten low-priority parts to stay inside the budget.
usage_notes: Route any new prompt through the shared fitting module and add its assembly point and fixtures to the evaluation so its budget is checked.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Guarded model-verdict judge
scoped_purpose: Use for: settling one narrow question (reach, quest choice, overseer signal, sufficiency) with a small model call and using the answer only when it is well formed. Avoid: letting a missing, malformed or hallucinated verdict change a turn, and broad open-ended decisions.
knowledge: Each judge has a deterministic half (parsing, gating, fallback order, digest budget, coverage of abridged reads) that can break independently of the model, so it is tested with a scripted provider. Digest shedding order protects the evidence the refusal rule needs. What the model decides is measured elsewhere.
measures_of_success: All labelled cases of parsing, gating, fallback order, digest budget and abridged-read coverage hold, and any provider failure leaves the turn unchanged. Standing conditions: Never let an unusable verdict alter behaviour, give the model the evidence its question depends on, and keep each judge's deterministic halves exact.
parameters: Per judge: the model tier, the digest budget, the fallback order and home quest for ranking, and whether web access is configured for the reach block.
inputs: A raw model answer or a failure, plus the judge's evidence (digest parts, candidate quests, executed reads and cards).
outputs: A parsed verdict (signal, reach verdict, quest ranking or the pending abridged items and notice), or the safe default.
effects: One small model call per judgment; no other writes; never raises.
usage_notes: Wire each judge through the orchestrator judges module, always supply a deterministic fallback, and test parsing against hostile outputs.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Reply safety and anticipation guards
scoped_purpose: Use for: stripping unverified links from replies, recognising a repeated operation without confusing a near miss, and offering recurring asks as suggestions when they recur. Avoid: sending any link that has not been proven, writing on a lookalike request, and suggesting patterns that are not strong enough.
knowledge: A model wrote plausible links to addresses that did not exist and readers lost trust, so every reply is scanned until a fixed point with unknown treated as dead. One network reading is noisy, so unknown results are retried. The link policy comes from the host, so the guard itself knows nothing about any one app.
measures_of_success: Fabricated links are removed and real ones kept, labels are extracted correctly, recipes match only true repeats, and chips appear at the right time with correct weights. Standing conditions: Send no unverified link, never write on a lookalike request, and show suggestion chips only when a pattern is strong, with sound match and weight arithmetic.
parameters: A link policy (trusted hosts, own origins, route table, in-app schemes, rewrite rules, passes and timeout), the recipe match score and scope tags, and the anticipation prune weight.
inputs: Reply text, a fetcher for link checks, learned requests with their tools and arguments, a past-asks history, and the current time.
outputs: Sanitised text with a verdict per link, extracted links and labels, a recipe match or learn count, chip texts, and updated weights.
effects: Network probes for links with a per-instance cache; recipe and pattern stores update when learning; replies are rewritten.
usage_notes: Run every terminal reply through the link guard before sending, supply the host's policy, and keep the guard offline-testable with an injected fetcher.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Incremental context-update feed
scoped_purpose: Use for: telling an assistant what is new on a work item since it last looked, from several channels such as notes, goal updates and decisions, offering each human-authored item once. Avoid: semantic retrieval of older background, judging whether an item is relevant to the topic, and acting on the items.
knowledge: A live run once treated a habit log and a daily reflection as asks and later reported them as still owed, so channels declare whether they carry asks. A reply written after a note is not proof the note was handled, and an assistant hearing its own words echoed back wastes budget. Card-scoped channels are relevant by where they were written, while user-scoped ones need a relevance judgment.
measures_of_success: The exact set of offered items and open asks matches the stated rules on synthetic quests: own words in, assistant echoes and unattributed notes out, answered and seen items not repeated, bounds respected. Standing conditions: Keep age and count bounds holding.
parameters: A source declares a name, a one-line description, and flags for whether its items need a relevance judgment, an admission judgment, tracking as asks, or relaying onto the work item. The engine takes the sources to watch, the channels always checked, and a clock; a collect call takes the item, an optional since time and the delivered-run history.
inputs: A collect request naming the work item and the time of the last look, plus whatever the channel's client returns (notes, goal updates, decisions, and similar).
outputs: A bundle of context updates, each with an item id, its text and author, and whether it needs a response, plus the set of open asks.
effects: Advances the watermark of what has been seen and may record asks for later tracking. Sources never raise: a source that fails reports an empty result and says why.
usage_notes: Call at the start of a turn or task for a work item and render the bundle into the prompt. Add a channel by implementing the source interface and setting its flags honestly, since a wrong asks flag turns a person's diary into owed answers.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Verbatim feedback ledger
scoped_purpose: Use for: remembering each correction a person gives, in their own words with author and time, and tracking how far it has been followed. Avoid: paraphrasing or summarising the correction, deciding which guidance applies to a turn, and grading the correction.
knowledge: Replying is not doing: a timestamp after a note closes it whether or not it was honoured, so status comes from the run's own structured disposition, and an unrecognised disposition leaves the item untouched. A person's status always outranks a run's. A standing rule is never finished by one application, so it stays in force and carries how far it has got; it is also written to a guidance card so retrieval carries it forward.
measures_of_success: A correction appears in the ledger as given, a standing rule becomes a guidance card shown on later turns, and a one-time request or the uncarded half of a mixed note never reaches guidance. Standing conditions: Keep every correction stored verbatim with author and time. Keep corrections across restarts. Keep one-time requests separate from standing rules.
parameters: The ledger takes an optional file path, a read-only flag, a flag requiring human acceptance before a run's done counts, and an optional pluggable store. Items carry card, source, item id, author, text, kind (request or standing), state and history.
inputs: Observed items (the person's words, author, time, source) and a run's account of what it did with each, opened by a disposition from a fixed vocabulary.
outputs: Ledger items with status lines, the open and standing sets, and guidance written for standing rules.
effects: Persists the whole document atomically and may write a guidance card per standing rule. A store that cannot be reached degrades to nothing recorded on read and a logged, swallowed failure on write.
usage_notes: Observe items when they arrive, record the run's account after each run, and let the guidance bridge carry standing rules. Supply a database-backed store when the host's durable record is not a file.
verdict_detail: passes more cases than dump_all; passes more cases than no_memory

name: Scoped recent-context warm start
scoped_purpose: Use for: handing the next turn the cards the last turns of the same conversation or work item already found relevant, so a short follow-up needs no restating and a timed-out assembly still has context. Avoid: full semantic retrieval, ranking by meaning, and any card from another work item or a stale one.
knowledge: Cards are re-selected from scratch each turn under a short budget, so a follow-up paid full cost and a timeout left a turn with nothing. Scope tags fence one work item's records from another's, while untagged legacy records stay visible. A purely lexical gate misses a paraphrase that shares no word, which is a known limit.
measures_of_success: On synthetic multi-turn cases the right earlier cards come back for a follow-up, and no stale or cross-work-item card is ever returned. Standing conditions: Keep stale and cross-work-item cards from being returned. Spend no model call.
parameters: The file store takes a root directory and caps for turns, cards, preview length, record age and items per card, with separate larger caps for the global scope. Scope keys name a conversation, a work item or the global scope.
inputs: For record: scope keys, the selected cards and the user's text. For load: scope keys, then the current turn's text for filtering.
outputs: Recent card records merged across scopes, narrower scope winning, deduplicated by card id, then filtered by relevance, with optional item-usage hints and rendered blocks.
effects: Writes small per-scope files atomically. Both calls are best effort and never raise.
usage_notes: Record after each turn that selected cards and load at the start of the next. Always pass the work item's key so the fence applies, and treat the result as a warm fallback beside, not instead of, normal retrieval.
verdict_detail: passes more cases than last_turn

name: Conversation-keyed mid-run input inbox
scoped_purpose: Use for: letting a person add direction, stop or pause while the assistant works, and having a message reach the next decision of the planner or of the running worker exactly once, for its own run. Avoid: ordering across conversations, and deciding how to respond to the message.
milestones: 1. Exactly-once mid-run delivery per run, and how fast it is seen: send-to-seen latency, acted-on share, stop-to-quiet time and cost per run recorded for the stream_json runner on live runs (3, then 10, then 30 runs, cheapest model first).
knowledge: Interfaces used to hand-wire pending-input callables, so one generic, application-agnostic inbox replaced them. A running deep worker CAN be re-prompted: Claude Code's stream-json session takes a user message on stdin while a tool runs and reads it at its next step (0.4 s after that tool finished in a probe on this machine, 2026-10-19), and takes an interrupt that stops the running step and keeps the session. The one-shot subprocess runner cannot, so there a message is seen only at the next attempt boundary; the stream_json deep runner (run-deep-work) is the alternative that closes that gap. A priority flag documented to move running work to the background did not do so in the probe, so only the default priority is used.
measures_of_success: A message pushed before or during a run reaches the next planner decision once, only for its own conversation, through a real orchestrator, and the port contract holds. For a deep worker with a live session: every message is written once and only to its own run (two concurrent runs never cross), one that lands as the run finishes is delivered once or left unclaimed, none is lost (a message written but not confirmed seen comes back as unseen), and work finished before a stop or pause is kept. Measured next to those: send-to-seen latency (p50 and p90 seconds, from the push to the model receiving it), acted-on share (steer cases whose required change happened, checked deterministically), stop-to-quiet time (from the stop request to the last tool event) and cost per run (dollars the run reports). Standing conditions: Deliver every pushed message to the next decision of the planner or of the running worker, exactly once, only for its own run. Lose none silently.
parameters: No tuning parameters: the contract is three calls keyed by a conversation id (push, drain, peek). A distributed implementation chooses its own storage settings.
inputs: A conversation id and a message string on push; a conversation id on drain and peek.
outputs: Drain returns and removes the pending messages in arrival order; peek returns them without removing.
effects: Drain empties that conversation's queue. The orchestrator drains between goal-loop steps when an inbox is wired.
usage_notes: Push once per incoming message from whatever interface receives it and wire the same inbox into the orchestrator. Supply a shared implementation when several processes serve one conversation.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Fail-safe card reference resolver
scoped_purpose: Use for: turning a typed pointer inside a context card (a note, a file, a record in the host's own store) into current text within a character budget when the card is read. Avoid: fetching data the library should not know about, summarising content, and letting one bad pointer break assembly.
knowledge: Notes and files ship with the library, while collection, conversation and query types hit the host's data layer, which the library must stay ignorant of, so the host injects them and its entries win. Resolution must never raise, because a failure at read time would break the whole assembly.
measures_of_success: Every pointer type resolves or renders a clear unresolved line, a failing resolver costs nothing else, and budgets and caps hold on the offline cases. Standing conditions: Return fresh text within the character budget. Render an unresolvable pointer as a stated unresolved line. Keep one failure from costing anything else.
parameters: Each resolver takes a locator and a maximum character count. The registry builder takes an optional file reader and a map of host resolvers, either objects or plain callables.
inputs: A locator dictionary describing the pointer, an item type, and the character budget.
outputs: Rendered text for the pointer, possibly marked abridged, or a short unresolved-pointer line.
effects: None beyond reading the source; a failing resolver is contained and returns empty text.
usage_notes: Build the registry once with the host's resolvers and pass it to the card renderer. Register a resolver for every type the host's cards use, since an unregistered type only shows its pointer.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Offline card cache and write outbox
scoped_purpose: Use for: keeping an assistant useful when the card backend is unreachable by serving the last known listing and holding failed writes for replay. Avoid: masking the outage, serving stale data silently, and sharing one cache between hosts.
knowledge: The repository never depends on a cache for correctness, and every backend failure is logged, counted and surfaced as a degraded status. A cold start during an outage is the case that separates a durable cache from a memory one. A file cache is single-host.
measures_of_success: On a card API that can go down, callers see identical behaviour, the stored listing is served on a cold start, and every failed write is replayed. Standing conditions: Keep caller-visible behaviour the same with or without a cache. Keep the outage loud. Keep the listing across restarts. Lose no failed write.
parameters: A cache is passed to the repository as an optional argument; the file cache takes a directory. The seam has no tuning parameters.
inputs: A full or delta listing with its latest update time, and failed writes as card id, card and team id.
outputs: The stored listing with its update time, or none, and the queued writes oldest first.
effects: Stores the listing and an outbox on each call; the durable cache writes files atomically and swallows its own I/O errors.
usage_notes: Choose the durable cache for any lane that must survive an outage across restarts; keep the null cache where failing loudly is wanted. Check the repository's health status to see degradation.
verdict_detail: passes as many cases as memory_cache at spend within 10% (or lower), so the metric does not separate them

name: Standing-instruction behaviour layer
scoped_purpose: Use for: making an assistant working on the repository follow evolvable-structure principles in its replies, such as naming the problem, defining an ideal and metric, reusing what exists and not over-building. Avoid: enforcing structure in code, adding structure when a small fix is right, and grading by vocabulary.
milestones: 1. Principle-following pass rate: recorded on the full set once the stratified sample stops moving between recordings.
knowledge: The standing instructions are generated from the skill and loaded by the deep run, so the shipped arm is the one that matters even when the metric cannot separate it from a plain prompt. Sampled, model-judged runs move by several cases between recordings, so small leads are noise. The judge and replies come from the same small model, and the in-situ setting has no tools so it scores a stated plan, not a diff.
measures_of_success: A larger share of scenario replies passes the model judge with the instructions than without, in both a chat setting and the deep-run prompt, with reference good replies passing and bad ones failing. Standing conditions: Keep replies from adding structure whose cost outweighs its benefit. Keep token cost of the instructions low.
parameters: The evaluation model and judge model are chosen by environment settings; each arm is a function from a case to a reply. The instructions are a markdown file synced from the skill.
inputs: A scenario text with its expected behaviour and failure mode.
outputs: A reply, then a pass or fail verdict with a one-line reason from the judge.
effects: Real model calls that cost money, metered per run, with no repository change.
usage_notes: Run on a stratified subset with a call cap. Treat a lead inside the margin as a tie and prefer the arm that matches what actually ships.
verdict_detail: within the stated margin of insitu_plain: pass rate inside 10 percentage points and spend inside 15% (sampled, model-judged runs move that much between re-runs), so the metric does not separate them

name: Behaviour-grading judge
scoped_purpose: Use for: grading whether a reply does what an evolvable-structure principle asks, by what it does rather than its vocabulary. Avoid: judging general quality, rewarding length or polish, and replacing a human reviewer.
milestones: 1. Judge agreement with labelled reference replies: agreement recorded against Joshua's verdicts, and for the regex_only baseline arm beside it.
knowledge: Vocabulary alone can fool a check, so the model judge is told to grade what the reply does and extra polish earns nothing. A reply that states the exact edit counts even when no tools were available. The labels come from the case author who also wrote the regexes, so agreement shows the judge is not broken, not that it matches a human reading. An unparseable answer must count as a fail.
measures_of_success: Good reference replies pass and bad ones fail, with few false passes and false fails, over the behaviour cases. Standing conditions: Keep cost to one cheap call per reply.
parameters: The judge model is set by environment settings with a cheap default; the judge receives the case's expected behaviour and failure mode and a reply length cap.
inputs: A behaviour case (scenario, expected behaviour, failure mode) and a reply.
outputs: A verdict of pass or fail with a one-line reason.
effects: One model call per reply for the model judge, metered; none for the regex floor.
usage_notes: Use the model judge for scoring replies and keep the regex check only as a cheap prefilter. Recalibrate against human verdicts when they exist.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

area: 9 Be adoptable and safe in the open
name: Public package surface contract
scoped_purpose: Use for: giving a consumer a package whose documented names import, whose registrations take effect, whose front doors build clients and configs from a clean environment, and whose shared helpers behave. Avoid: consumer-specific logic, network access at import time, and model calls.
knowledge: The package root is the one place that sees core, adapters and runner, so it wires what core needs without core importing them. Vendored editing code is kept because most of it absorbs specific ways real models get the format wrong, and an approximation would lose that quietly. A test shows a broken implementation that merely imports each name fails the cases.
measures_of_success: Public names, version, registrations, front-door outcomes, async bridge, signature probes, reply strippers, report builders, offline imports and vendored edit cases all pass. Standing conditions: Make every documented name import. Make every registration and front door take effect on fixture inputs. Need no network or model to import.
parameters: Front doors take an optional config file path and a timeout; the async bridge takes a coroutine or a blocking function with arguments. No other tuning exists.
inputs: A config path or environment for the front doors; coroutines or callables for the bridge; text for the edit parser.
outputs: A configured client or runner config, results of bridged calls, parsed edit blocks and applied edits.
effects: The package root installs core wiring at import; the bridge starts one long-lived background loop; nothing opens a network connection at import.
usage_notes: Import from the package root and use the front doors rather than re-deriving environment variable names. Add a case whenever a new name enters the docs.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Runnable example set
scoped_purpose: Use for: letting a newcomer learn the library from small examples that still compile, import, run their offline path, are introduced in the examples index, and leak nothing. Avoid: examples needing live services in this check, and teaching by prose alone.
knowledge: Three consumers once each hand-wrote the same lane driver, so the minimal example shows how little a lane must supply once the shared driver and config exist. Examples read everything from the environment with placeholders. Demos that need a live backend or a terminal can only be scored on import, refusal to start and stub behaviour.
measures_of_success: Each example compiles, imports, reaches its help or not-configured exit in a scrubbed environment, appears in the index, and passes the secret and path scan. Standing conditions: Keep every example runnable on an empty environment. Keep each introduced in the index. Keep secrets and machine paths out.
parameters: Each example takes its own command-line modes (check, once, loop) and reads configuration from a file layered under environment variables, with the environment winning.
inputs: A config file and environment variables; no secrets are baked in.
outputs: A running lane or a built runner configuration, and help or not-configured messages on an empty environment.
effects: The lane example may poll a backend when configured; offline paths have none.
usage_notes: Copy the minimal lane to start, adapt the custom consumer for a specific organisation, and add a file to the index in the same change.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Queued-task runner lane
scoped_purpose: Use for: taking a task someone queued for the assistant to a reported outcome, claimed once, run by the right persona, and reported done, failed or needing the person. Avoid: running a task twice, dropping it, running it before its time, and deciding what the task should be.
knowledge: Discovery is event driven with signature dedup across restarts and a backend-aware claim as a second guard. A persona activates only when asked for, never from a bare mention of a name. Folder sync keeps human text and pushes each bullet once. Cancelled tasks need no patch because the backend already set the status.
measures_of_success: Poll, claim, run and report behave correctly across done, failed, needs-you, duplicate, lost-claim, not-yet-due, team-scoped and unconfigured cases, with persona choice, folder sync and scheduling correct. Standing conditions: Claim each due task once. Run it as the right persona against its work folder. Report an outcome for every task. Run none early.
parameters: The poller takes a configuration with credentials, team, adapters and a concurrency bound; personas take a skills root, registry, assignment fields and flags for model-judged asks; the lane driver takes check, once or loop modes and an env file.
inputs: Queued tasks from the backend, the configuration, persona registry and folder map.
outputs: A reported status on each task (with result text or decision id), updated folder sync files, and logs.
effects: Claims tasks on the backend, writes the sync file in work folders, may post notes, and spawns deep runs.
usage_notes: Start a lane with the shared driver and pick one-shot mode for cron or loop mode for a service. Use structured assignment for personas where tasks name an owner.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Layered lane configuration loader
scoped_purpose: Use for: turning a configuration file plus environment variables into one validated runner configuration at startup, with a defined precedence between sources. Avoid: wiring adapters from the resulting configuration, and per-request or per-turn overrides.
knowledge: A lane is operated by people who edit a file and export variables, so a silent typo or a surprising winner between sources costs a deployment. Past design lessons: the file is a baseline, the core package must never read the process environment directly, and tuning values must tolerate bad input by falling back to defaults so a running process can be retuned without a restart.
measures_of_success: Every precedence rule holds in every probed combination, every invalid key is refused loudly before the lane starts, and a bad tuning value never stops the lane.
parameters: A path to a TOML file (or none), plus the set of file-expressible fields owned by the configuration dataclass; tuning values are read from an optional environment mapping.
inputs: The configuration file text, additional environment files it references, the process environment, and the environment tables inside the file.
outputs: A populated runner configuration object, or a configuration-file error naming the offending key; tuning values come back as one typed settings value.
effects: Exports file-defined environment values into the process environment where the precedence rules allow, and installs the tuning-settings provider used by the core package.
usage_notes: Call at startup, before building any adapter; use the file for baselines and environment variables for per-deployment overrides. Add a file-expressible field only together with its precedence or validation rule.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

area: 9 Be adoptable and safe in the open
name: Non-interactive command-line surface
scoped_purpose: Use for: letting a person or a deep run's shell invoke the runner and its tool catalog through subcommands with stable parsing, output and exit codes. Avoid: the interactive chat terminal, the poll loop, the channel and file-serving surfaces, which need a terminal or a server.
knowledge: A deep run reaches the same tools through a shell, so the command line is a fixed contract that other processes depend on. Design lessons: write-capable methods must be refused unless explicitly allowed, maintenance commands default to a dry run, and missing credentials must produce a message that says what to set.
measures_of_success: Every subcommand answers help, unknown commands and flags and malformed arguments are refused with the usage code, write methods are refused without the write flag, and the tool catalog lists, shows and calls tools correctly.
parameters: A subcommand with its flags; the quest command takes a method name and keyword pairs, the context commands take store locations and an apply flag, the tool entry point takes list, show or call with keyword or JSON arguments.
inputs: The argument vector, the process environment for credentials, and files or a store folder the command points at.
outputs: Text on standard output and error and an integer exit code, with zero for success and the usage code for a refused invocation.
effects: Write subcommands change Quest data or card stores only when explicitly allowed; context maintenance commands are dry runs unless an apply flag is given.
usage_notes: Use from scripts and from a deep run's shell; prefer the read-only form first, add the write or apply flag deliberately, and add a case when a subcommand or flag is added.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Cost-ordered model tier selector with outage and allowance recovery
scoped_purpose: Use for: choosing which model rung starts a piece of work, resolving a family or tier name to the newest live release, falling back when a tier is exhausted, and recognising provider outages and usage limits so work resumes later. Avoid: judging whether the cheapest model still succeeded, which needs live runs, and the routing of a message itself.
knowledge: The planner already rates difficulty on the call that decides the route, so starting-model choice costs no extra model call. Past incidents: queued tasks failed outright when a provider briefly overloaded and had to be rerun by hand, and a subscription allowance limit looks like a failed run rather than an outage, so each needs its own recognition and a resume time.
measures_of_success: Each difficulty maps to the stated starting rung, family names track new releases without edits, a pin always wins, an exhausted tier falls to the next cheaper one, and outages and limits are recognised with a correct resume time.
parameters: A difficulty rating, a ladder of rungs, optional operator model mapping and pins, a tier or family name, the list of live models, and the current time for limit parsing.
inputs: The planner's difficulty rating, a provider's live model list, error or result text from a failed model call, and the clock.
outputs: A starting model and ladder, a concrete model id for a tier or family, the next lower tier, a vision-capability answer, an outage verdict, and a usage-limit record with its reset and resume times.
effects: Remembers the latest outage and usage limit lane-wide, optionally persisted to a file, so other tasks hold off until the resume time.
usage_notes: Resolve names through the registry at the point of use rather than pinning release ids; set an operator pin only when a specific model is required. Treat an outage as a reason to requeue, not to fail the task.
verdict_detail: no rival implementation was measured on the same cases

name: Cost estimation, daily budget and host load guard
scoped_purpose: Use for: estimating what an operation will cost before it spends, stopping new work at a daily token budget, and pausing pickup when the host is overloaded. Avoid: output-token billing, real provider invoices, and work done by a subscription-based deep runner, which does not count toward the budget.
knowledge: Shallow orchestrator calls can run away on cost, so a daily cap is opt-in and persisted. Pausing pickup is lossless because unclaimed tasks stay queued and fire on a later scan. Prices are a hand-kept snapshot of list prices, so a provider change is not noticed until the table is edited.
measures_of_success: Prices and estimates are arithmetically right, the daily total survives a restart and resets each day, bad or negative values are handled, and the guard pauses and resumes without flapping.
parameters: Provider and model names, a token count, daily limit and usage path from the environment, and optional host limits for memory percent, free memory and load.
inputs: Token counts per call, environment variables, and host samples of memory and load.
outputs: A price per million input tokens, a bootstrap cost estimate with the provider and model used, a running total with an over-limit flag and status line, and a paused or not verdict.
effects: Writes the day's tally to a usage file and signals the poller to stop picking up new tasks while over budget or overloaded; in-flight tasks are never killed.
usage_notes: Both limits are opt-in; set them per lane. Review the price table whenever a provider changes prices.

name: Public-repository hygiene scanner
scoped_purpose: Use for: finding secrets, real machine paths, object ids and real addresses in working files before they are committed to a public repository. Avoid: scanning git history, and detecting a secret shape the scanner has no pattern for.
knowledge: A public repository must hold nothing consumer specific or secret, and documentation needs to show the shape of a secret without being flagged, so placeholders are explicitly allowed. A secret already committed must be rotated, since the scan does not read history. Findings print a redacted snippet, never the whole secret.
measures_of_success: Every planted secret kind is found, every documented placeholder stays quiet, the repository scans clean, and the command exits with failure on any finding.
parameters: A repository root, an option to scan only staged files, and optional file selection.
inputs: Text or files known to git (tracked, or untracked and not ignored).
outputs: A list of findings with a pattern name, a location and a redacted snippet, and an exit code that is nonzero on any finding.
effects: None; it reads files only and changes nothing.
usage_notes: Run before every commit, including staged-only mode in a commit step. Add a pattern and a planted test case together whenever a new credential shape appears.
